Figure 2:NEO-VLA: pixels in, continuous actions out.Previous and current multi-view observations preserve their aspect ratios within a fixed token budget and enter patch embedder shared across time and views. The visual path uses no vision transformer, autoencoder, or vector-quantised codebook. Shared MLPs embed camera intrinsics and rotations, while state MLPs embed previous and current robot states. These tokens join a
structured prompt describing control frequency, embodiment, frame reference, and task instruction.
A separate, narrow, randomly initialised action expert jointly attends to cached prefix keys and values from selected backbone layers and its own action-token keys and values. Its suffix embeddings combine projected noisy actions and flow timeτ\tauwith additive step, frame, and identity embeddings.
Both arm blocks and the body block share temporal rotary offsets00–2929, with identity embeddings distinguishing the blocks. Trained by flow matching, the expert predicts a velocity field that covers both arm and body action chunks.

Figure 5:Real-world manipulation benchmark.(a) Place a tennis ball on a can.
(b) Place a tape roll in a bowl, then place a tennis ball inside the roll.
(c) Reorient a horizontal can and insert it upright into a tape roll.
The tasks test placement precision, multi-step execution, and object reorientation. Each model is fine-tuned on 50 episodes per scene and evaluated over 20 trials.

Figure 6:Real-world NEO-VLA demonstrations.(a) Pick up a paper cup and pour water into a glass.
(b) Place a tennis ball on a can.
(c) Place a tape roll in a bowl, then place the ball inside the roll.
(d) Reorient a horizontal can and insert it upright into a tape roll.
(e) Pick four gunkan sushi pieces, one at a time, from a table of mixed sushi and place them on a plate.
Frames are arranged chronologically from left to right, with dashed circles highlighting key interaction moments and critical manipulation steps.
